newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala tourist plane crash kills 14.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala tourist plane crash kills 14.

text.p: Fourteen people, including an American woman, were killed when a small plane flying tourists to the Mayan ruins of Tikal crashed in thick jungle on Friday morning, officials said.

The Brazilian-made Bandeirante turboprop plane was on a regular tourist flight from Guatemala City to Tikal and crashed as it prepared to land, Juan Luis Munoz, head of operations at the Guatemala City aviation authority, said.
Munoz told Reuters there were no survivors of the crash and two crew members were among the 14 dead.

"The aircraft was totally destroyed. Only small pieces of the plane were left. The passengers were completely incinerated. Only one could be fully identified," said Felipe Mejia, the National Police duty officer at the Santa Elena airport, where the plane was due to land.

Aviation authority officials said the bodies of the victims, including two children and a U.S. woman, were taken to a local hospital and may be moved later to Guatemala City for identification by family members.
The plane belonged to local airline Transportes Aereos Profesionales (TAPSA) and was preparing to land at Santa Elena, which serves the world famous Mayan temple site of Tikal, when it crashed.

Tikal draws thousands of tourists from around the globe to marvel at its well-preserved Mayan ruins, located in spectacular unspoiled rainforest inhabited mainly by spider monkeys, lizards, snakes and quetzal birds.

Officials at the Guatemalan civil aviation authority said the plane crashed in cloudy weather about five miles (eight km) from its destination in Peten province near Guatemala's northern border with Mexico.

Jorge Perez, chief of flight operations at the Santa Elena airport, said another plane crashed in the same place 10 years ago and access was not difficult because the area of thick jungle was partially cleared out.
According to Perez, the site of the accident was just over a mile (1.8 km) from a highway.
According to a spokesman for the TAPSA airline, who declined to be identified, the victims were all Guatemalans except for American Ana Deborah Young. No home town for Young was available.

The crash was the second involving a Guatemalan aircraft in just over a year. On Aug. 9 of last year, a Boeing 737 belonging to the country's Aviateca airline slammed into a volcano in El Salvador, killing all 65 people aboard.

It was also the second accident on that route in less than three years. On Nov. 22, 1993 13 people were killed, including U.S., German and Canadian tourists, when a twin engine plane returning from Tikal to Guatemala City crashed 30 miles (53 km) north of the capital.

Friday's accident was also the second major disaster to hit Guatemala in the last month. On Oct. 16 at least 80 people were crushed to death at a soccer stadium in Guatemala City just before the kickoff of a World Cup qualifying soccer match between Guatemala and Costa Rica.
